title: A guest at the Friday table
hook: invited to a Friday-night dinner for the first time: what happens, and what nobody expects of you
carry: you don't have to know the words

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shalom Aleichem: the song for the two angels who walk you home. Your line was angels walk you home. Today, someone else is walking through the door: a guest. Day one hundred one.

The text says: come for Shabbat dinner, Friday, seven. Maybe it's your partner's parents. Maybe a coworker, a college Hillel, a friend who just started hosting. Maybe you're Jewish and have never actually been to one. And the questions start. What do I bring? Do I need to know Hebrew? What if everyone stands up and I'm still sitting? Here's the good news first: a Friday table is built for guests. Inviting people, especially people with nowhere else to go, is one of the oldest parts of Shabbat. Today: what to expect when you're the one walking in.
screen: `COME FOR SHABBAT DINNER.` → `DO I NEED HEBREW?` → `A TABLE BUILT FOR GUESTS.`

segments.voice: Start at the door. The greeting is Shabbat shalom, a peaceful Sabbath. In some homes you'll hear the Yiddish, gut Shabbos. Either is perfect. Come on time, or a little early, because in many homes the candles are lit before sunset, and in observant homes the host won't drive, cook, or answer the phone once Shabbat begins. Flowers are a safe gift. If you'd like to bring food or wine, ask first, since many hosts keep kosher. Then the evening has an order, and most of it is joyful. A song, often Shalom Aleichem. In many homes, parents bless their children. Then Kiddush, the blessing over a cup of wine or grape juice; some families stand for it, some sit, and you just do what the table does. Then the part that surprises guests. Many people get up and wash their hands at a sink, pouring water from a cup, and then go quiet. Nobody's upset. There's a custom of not talking between washing and the blessing over the bread, so the two stay joined. Then the challah is blessed, often sprinkled with salt, torn and passed around. And then dinner, which can go on for hours. What nobody expects of you: to know the Hebrew, to sing along, or to pretend to be anything you're not. Listening is enough. Asking is better. What's this for? is a question most hosts are delighted to answer. The rabbis even taught that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. You're not intruding on the evening. You're part of what it's for.
screen: `SHABBAT SHALOM AT THE DOOR.` · `CANDLES, SONG, BLESSINGS, WINE.` · `WASH, THEN A QUIET MOMENT.` · `NOBODY EXPECTS THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk in as a guest. Settle, and breathe. Picture a front door on a Friday evening. You ring, and someone opens it, smiling. You say Shabbat shalom. Inside, candles are already burning on the table. Picture being handed a seat, a cup, a piece of torn bread. Notice whatever nervousness comes up, and let it soften. Nobody at this table is grading you. If you're usually the host, picture welcoming one person who'd be alone on a Friday night. The bell holds the time.
Shabbat shalom. A peaceful Sabbath: the greeting at the door on Friday night, for hosts and guests alike.
Your line: you don't have to know the words. A guest who shows up and asks good questions is doing it right. Day one hundred one.

howItsDone: Many Jewish families and communities invite guests for Friday-night dinner, including friends, partners and people who would otherwise be alone; guests are welcome to follow along, ask questions and join in as much or as little as they like.

fork.setup: you're a guest. everyone washes their hands and suddenly nobody's talking. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and follow along until the bread is blessed.
fork.reveal: many families keep quiet between washing the hands and the blessing over bread, so the two stay joined. the talking comes right back with the challah.

original.note: Hebrew: a peaceful Sabbath, the Friday-night greeting.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dinner party with prayers you won't understand.
what it means: a table with an order, built to welcome guests, where nobody expects you to know the words.

what a scholar hears: the Talmud (Shabbat 127a) says welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, learned from Abraham running to the strangers; the quiet after washing follows the principle that the blessing over bread comes right after washing (Berakhot 42a).

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127a (welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 42a (the blessing follows the washing of hands immediately)

notes: Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper.

Replaces 'Blessing the children', which repeated day 75 (Blessing the grandsons) nearly point for point: Ephraim and Manasseh, the same two reasons, the four mothers and the priestly blessing. That content still lives in day 75, and this lesson mentions that many parents bless their children on Friday night.

Why: the research names interfaith partners and non-Jewish guests (and Jews who never went to one) as a large part of the audience, asking 'what do I need to know before I'm invited?'; the current curriculum had one day on interfaith families, in year 3 (day 1049).
Order of the Friday table (Shalom Aleichem, blessing the children, Kiddush, washing, hamotzi) is the common Ashkenazi order; customs vary. Confirm.
The no-talking custom between netilat yadayim and hamotzi is described as a custom; confirm framing and the Berakhot 42a source (tekef linetilat yadayim beracha).
Guest tips (arrive before candle-lighting, flowers are safe, ask before bringing food or wine, observant hosts don't drive or use phones on Shabbat) are general practice, not law; confirm wording.
The Talmud line (Shabbat 127a: greater is hospitality than receiving the Shekhinah) is paraphrased; it was also taught on day 43.
